full_judgment:
Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, J.—This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner is directed against an order passed by the learned Munsif staying execution of a decree passed in a title suit for declaration of title and recovery of possession. 

 It appears that a title suit for declaration of title and for recovery of possession was instituted by the plaintiff which was decreed on contest on 14.9.66 and on appeal the suit was remanded for re-hearing and was again decreed on contest on 20.6.68. On appeal, the decree was affirmed and thereafter the second appeal preferred by the defendants being S.A. No. 150 of 1971 was dismissed on contest by an order of this Court on 5.3.76. 

 2. The Title Execution Case No. 8 of 1971 arising out of the said decree was stayed by this Court in Civil Rule No. 371 (s) of 1971 which was, however, discharged and the order of stay vacated by this Court on 5.3.76 along with the dismissal of the connected second appeal. Thereafter, one of the defendants, namely, Azimunnessa who had also appeared in the second appeal filed an application for stay of the execution proceedings which was rejected by the executing court by order dated 14.5.76. Thereafter another application by the said defendant was similarly rejected on 23.6.76. The defendant Azimunnessa thereafter filed Title Suit No. 327 of 1976 for setting aside the decree passed in title suit on the ground of fraud and filed an application before the Executing Court on 6.8.76 for stay of the execution case. The Executing Court allowed the prayer and stayed further proceedings of the execution case. Hence the present rule at the instance of the plaintiffs. 

 4. According to the learned referring Judge the main question in the rule is whether the defendant could file a suit in the court below for a declaration that the ex-parte decree which was upheld and affirmed by the High Court was a nullity and secondly, whether the executing court could stay execution of a decree finally upheld by the High Court and lastly, whether the High Court was in a position to rectify any such irregularity, if any at all. 

 6. The second question raised by the learned Judge was whether the executing court could stay the execution of a decree affirmed by the High Court. The answer, in our view, is in the negative for the simple reason that the decree of the trial court having now finally got merged in the decree passed by this Court in the second appeal and the order staying further proceeding of the title execution case having been vacated by this Court, it was the clear duty of the executing court to proceed with the execution case in accordance with law. The court below by staying the execution case has clearly gone beyond its jurisdiction and competence. The impugned order, to all intents and purposes, amounts to overriding an order of a superior Court by a sub-ordinate court, a situation never contemplated in legal jurisprudence. It is now well settled that an executing court cannot go behind the decree except on the ground of territorial and pecuniary jurisdiction and within this very strict limits the executing court is competent to consider the question of legality or otherwise of a decree.
